haiku-low.q1: It returns the popular 20-item list with fallback true. Reason is lookup_timeout on a timeout, or no_features when the user has no row.
haiku-low.q2: It keeps using rows already in the store, up to 6 hours old, counted from source_as_of. After that rows count as missing and users fall back one by one.
haiku-low.q3: No. Shadow output is logged, never shown. Shadow failures never reach the user and never slow the response.
haiku-low.q4: Users whose hash(salt, user_id) bucket is under percentage×100, so under 1000 at 10%, and whose feature row satisfies the candidate manifest, after a successful active response.
haiku-low.q5: The version must be registered, eligible, and have an approval record naming a passing gate report. The gates require at least 7 days in shadow under one salt.
haiku-low.q6: NOT STATED as decided. The plan has no live A/B step. Product has not chosen between a live slice and going straight to 100%.
haiku-low.q7: Pool servers poll the serving config every 10 s, download and checksum the version, run warm-up, then atomically swap. API instances poll config every 10 s and read only the active version ID.
haiku-low.q8: The API queues a sample with the feature row after the response is written. A background worker sends the candidate's manifest features to the shadow pool with a 500 ms deadline, so no latency is added.
haiku-low.q9: The sample is dropped from the bounded per-instance queue, a counter increases, and nothing waits. Drops are not counted as attempts. Above 1% drop rate, the window is invalid.
haiku-low.q10: Each attempt is logged to a log stream, then an append-only warehouse table. A daily job compares overlap at 20, candidate errors, p99, drop rate, and coverage.
haiku-low.q11: The registry checks the manifest against the store's schema, and ineligible versions cannot be shadowed or activated. Per-request checks also refuse rows missing required features.
haiku-low.q12: An operator writes a CAS revision pointing active at the prior active version, with no approval needed. Pool servers keep the previous version in memory, so no download; the swap is under 5 s.

sonnet.q1: The popular-items list (20 item IDs) with fallback true and a reason: lookup_timeout (30 ms deadline missed), or no_features (no row). A store error gives lookup_error. The model is not called.
sonnet.q2: It uses whatever rows are already in the online store, checked on every read. Rows keep serving until they are older than 6 hours, measured from source_as_of. After that they count as stale (stale_features) and users fall back to the popular list one by one. An alert fires after 90 minutes with no successful run.
sonnet.q3: No. Shadow output is logged, never shown to the user. Shadow failures never reach the user or slow the response; they are counted as candidate failures.
sonnet.q4: Users in the shadow cohort: bucket = hash(salt, user_id) mod 10000 is below percentage x 100 (below 1000 at 10%). They must also have a successful active-model response (not a fallback), and their feature row must satisfy the candidate's manifest. The sample is queued only then.
sonnet.q5: It must be registered and eligible (all manifest features exist in the online store schema). It must have run at least 7 continuous days in shadow under one salt and candidate, and passed the gates: eligible for the whole window, error rate under 0.5%, candidate p99 under 80 ms, drop rate at or under 1%. The gate report must be stored and passing, and the ML lead must have recorded an approval for that version naming a passing report. An operator then writes a CAS config revision through the control tool, which checks all of this.
sonnet.q6: No. Whether to add a live A/B slice is an undecided product question. Nothing is built for it. The plan goes shadow to 100%, but the config shape leaves a slice possible later.
sonnet.q7: API instances poll the serving config every 10 s and keep the last good copy in memory. They only read the active version ID and send it with each request. They never load models. The pool servers poll too, then download the artifact, verify its checksum, run a warm-up inference and atomically swap the reference. No API redeploy is needed.
sonnet.q8: After a successful active response, the API queues a sample holding the feature row it already read for the active model. The shadow worker sends the feature values the candidate's manifest lists to the shadow pool, with a 500 ms deadline. Both models see the same values. It adds no latency because the sample is queued after the response bytes are written, and the worker runs in the background, off the request path.
sonnet.q9: Each instance has a bounded in-memory queue. If it is full, the sample is dropped, a counter goes up and nothing waits. Drops are counted separately, not as attempts. The shadow pool has its own concurrency limit, and shadow load is shed first when the active pool is busy. A drop rate above 1% marks the window invalid.
sonnet.q10: Every shadow attempt writes a record (request_id, user_id, candidate version, salt, active items, candidate items, candidate inference time, status, source_as_of, config revision). These go to a log stream, then an append-only warehouse table. A daily comparison job keeps only records matching the current candidate and salt, on or after started_at. It reports overlap at 20, candidate error rate, candidate p99, drop rate and eligible coverage. The document does not say where active-model predictions are recorded apart from the shadow records.
sonnet.q11: An eligibility check compares the version's manifest with the online store's current schema, at registration and whenever the store's schema changes. An ineligible version cannot be shadowed or activated, and the control tool refuses the config write. As a safety net, step 4 refuses rows lacking a required feature (feature_mismatch fallback). Step 6 checks the candidate manifest before queuing shadow samples. If the active version becomes ineligible, its pointer stays and users get the fallback until an operator switches or rolls back.
sonnet.q12: An operator writes a CAS config revision, through the control tool, that points active at the rollback target. That target is the version active in the previous revision, found in the config history. No approval is needed. It is fast because each active pool server keeps the current and previous version in memory, so no download is needed. The assumed budget is a 10 s poll, a swap under 5 s and confirmation under 30 s. If the target is no longer in memory, the normal load path runs.
